name: Hash Tables & Bloom Filters
tagline: O(1) key-value hash indexing paired with probabilistic Bloom bitsets that reject non-existent keys in RAM with zero false negatives.
purpose: Build a progressive mental model of hash tables and Bloom filters—from open addressing vs. chaining to Bloom filter sizing math (m, k, p) and protecting LSM-tree SSTables from disk I/O.

spark.summary: A Bloom filter is a space-efficient probabilistic data structure used to test set membership. It answers queries with "definitely not in set" (zero false negatives) or "probably in set" (with a tunable false positive rate). By eliminating expensive disk reads and database scans for non-existent keys, Bloom filters protect high-throughput databases like Cassandra, RocksDB, and HBase.
spark.keyTakeaway: Bloom filters have zero false negatives: if the filter returns false, the item is 100% guaranteed not to exist. Use them as an in-memory guard rail to bypass expensive disk I/O and network hops.
spark.byteSummary:
**Core Mechanics:** A **Hash Table** maps keys to values in `O(1)` average time using a hash function and collision resolution (separate chaining or open addressing).

**Visual & Structural Flow:** Depicts Bloom Filter RAM Guard Protecting LSM-Tree SSTable Disk Reads (Read: user_9999 -> In-Memory Bloom -> Any Bit == 0 -> Skip -> Disk SSTables); Scalable Bloom Filter Saturation & Chaining State Machine (HEALTHY (<50% Bits) -> SATURATED (>50%) -> CHAINED SLICE).

**Trade-Offs & Production:** Choose the membership structure based on deletion needs, space budget, and false-positive tolerance. When a static Bloom filter fills past ~50% set bits, its false-positive rate climbs exponentially (**Saturation Bit Fill Collapse**).

**Failure Modes & Application:** Explore how Bloom filters stop cache-penetration attacks and accelerate LSM-tree storage engines.

learningJourney.title: What are Hash Tables & Bloom Filters
learningJourney.explanation:
A **Hash Table** maps keys to values in `O(1)` average time using a hash function and collision resolution (separate chaining or open addressing). A **Bloom Filter** trades exact key storage for extreme space efficiency: it uses an `m`-bit array (all `0`s) and `k` independent hash functions.

On **insert**, hash the key `k` times and set those `k` bit positions to `1`. On **query**, check those `k` positions: if **any** bit is `0`, the key is **100% definitely not** in the set (zero false negatives). If all `k` bits are `1`, the key is **probably** in the set (tunable false-positive rate `p`).

sectionDiagram.title: Bloom Filter RAM Guard Protecting LSM-Tree SSTable Disk Reads

cards.label: Sizing Rule
cards.detail: 10 bits per key (m/n = 10) with k = 7 hashes yields a ~1% false positive rate.

cards.label: 0.1% Precision
cards.detail: 14.4 bits per key with k = 10 hashes drops false positives to 0.1%.

cards.label: No Deletion
cards.detail: Clearing a bit to 0 could break other colliding keys; use Counting or Cuckoo filters for deletes.

sectionDiagram.summary: Keeping ~10 bits per key in RAM eliminates 99% of wasted disk seeks on non-existent keys.

learningJourney.title: Why Databases & CDNs Need Bloom Filters in Front of Disk
learningJourney.explanation: Disk I/O is `10,000x` slower than RAM. In an LSM-tree cluster (RocksDB, Cassandra) with 100 SSTables on disk, looking up a non-existent key `user_9999` without a Bloom filter forces checking all 100 SSTable indexes (`45 ms`). With per-SSTable Bloom filters in RAM, 98+ SSTables are rejected in `0.1 ms`.

ideas.title: CDN One-Hit-Wonder Filtering
ideas.description: Akamai and Cloudflare place a Bloom filter in front of SSD caches so 'one-hit wonder' URLs are only written to flash on their *second* request, doubling SSD lifespan.

ideas.title: Optimal Sizing Formula
ideas.description: Given capacity `n` and target false-positive rate `p`: `m = -n * ln(p) / (ln(2)^2)` bits and `k = (m / n) * ln(2)` hash functions.

comparison.choice: Good Candidate: LSM-Tree SSTables & Cache Penetration Defense
benefits: Blocks malicious or random non-existent key floods from hitting PostgreSQL/disk.
costs: Requires contiguous bit allocation sized upfront for expected cardinality `n`.

benefits: Exact HashSet or B-tree guarantees zero false positives.
costs: A 1% false-positive rate in a blocklist or allowlist leaks or blocks 1% of valid users.

benefits: Cuckoo Filters or Counting Bloom Filters support `delete()` safely.
costs: Standard Bloom filters cannot delete keys without corrupting colliding bits.

learningJourney.title: Double-Hashing Bloom Filter Implementation & Saturation Guard
learningJourney.explanation: Instead of computing `k` separate cryptographic hashes, production filters (Kirsch-Mitzenmacher) compute just two 64-bit hashes `h1, h2` and derive `k` positions via `(h1 + i * h2) % m`.

learningJourney.title: Alternatives: Standard Bloom vs. Cuckoo Filter vs. Exact Hash Table
learningJourney.explanation: Choose the membership structure based on deletion needs, space budget, and false-positive tolerance.

benefits: ~10 bits/key for 1% FP; simplest, zero false negatives.
costs: No deletions; saturates if cardinality `n` exceeds initial estimate.

benefits: Supports `delete()`, better cache locality (2 buckets), and lower space at `<3%` FP.
costs: Insertions can fail/rehash if load factor exceeds ~95%.

benefits: Zero false positives and stores full key->value payloads.
costs: 10x–50x larger RAM footprint because full keys must be stored.

learningJourney.title: Production Safeguard: Saturation Monitoring & Scalable Chaining
learningJourney.explanation: When a static Bloom filter fills past ~50% set bits, its false-positive rate climbs exponentially (**Saturation Bit Fill Collapse**). Production systems monitor fill ratio and chain **Scalable Bloom Filters** (allocating a new, larger slice with tighter `fp_rate` whenever capacity is reached).

knowledgeCheck.question: A Bloom filter guarding a database returns `might_contain('user_9999') == False`. What can the database safely conclude?

options.text: `user_9999` is 100% guaranteed NOT to exist in that SSTable/set, so the disk read can be skipped
options.feedback: Correct: Bloom filters have zero false negatives—a `False` result is mathematically definitive.

options.text: `user_9999` has a 1% chance of existing on disk
options.feedback: The 1% error rate applies only to false *positives* (`True` when absent), never false negatives.

options.text: The filter is saturated and must be rebuilt immediately
options.feedback: Returning `False` means at least one hashed bit was `0`, which only happens on an unsaturated, healthy filter.
